name: Lena Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a die-cutter at a packaging plant out by the canal. Big sheets of corrugated cardboard go in, and the machine stamps them into boxes for pizza places, wine shops, online orders. I set up the cutting dies, feed the sheets, keep an eye on the stacks and clear jams, which happen more than they should. I like it because I know that machine better than anyone, all its noises. What wears me out is the dust, it gets in your hair, your ears, everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, outside of the plant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Marco, he's an electrician, mostly houses and small shops. We bought a flat together two years ago with a bit of help from his parents, and we've still got about eight months of money set aside on top. I'm not a big spender, I like a quiet weekend, a walk by the canal, his mum's Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I probably wouldn't say much, to be honest. I'm not really an online person. At work I'd maybe say to the guys, well, that's that then, and get back on the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be glad. I've never used any of those AI things, I don't see the point, and I'd be happy never to. I've spent six years learning one machine's moods. I don't want to start again with one that has opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Keep paying the mortgage, keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe do the kitchen next year like we planned. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one where nothing gets in the way of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't see the point of AI tools. Has anyone at work tried to get you to use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning office uses something to schedule the orders, I think. They tried to get us to use a tablet for logging jams and I kept using the paper sheet until they gave up. I'm not proud of it, but it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gets AI wrong, the people hyping it or the people dismissing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, probably. The people selling it make it sound like magic, and some of the older men at work talk like it's the devil. I just think most things end up somewhere in the middle.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, since I'm not an online person. At work I'd tell the others, well, that's that then, and get back on the machine.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd be glad, because I've never used AI and I don't want to start. I've spent six years learning one machine and I don't want to start over.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as before, paying the mortgage, saving a little each month and doing the kitchen renovation next year as planned.
S0.feel: Calm, because nothing gets in the way of her plans.
S0.quote: I've spent six years learning one machine's moods. I don't want to start again with one that has opinions.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is quiet, practical and openly avoids new technology, to the point of quietly outlasting a tablet rollout. She sits in the middle on who gets AI wrong. Her life plan is modest and already well funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like, well, we'll see, there's always change. I wouldn't make a big deal of it in public. If a manager asked, I'd say I'll learn what I need to learn, when I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried. Die-cutters are already pretty automatic on the new models, they feed themselves. If the plant buys one of those, the job becomes watching a screen, and I'd be rubbish at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot at first. I'd keep my head down and do my job well, and I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe push the kitchen back a year. If they bought a new machine, I'd do the training they gave me, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear the boss is visiting the factory floor and nobody knows why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be rubbish at watching a screen. Why do you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learn with my hands and my ears. I can hear a jam coming two seconds before it happens. I can't hear a screen. I'd be slower, and I'd hate feeling slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got plenty of similar plants nearby. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. There are three box plants within twenty minutes, so if mine changed I could probably go somewhere still running the old machines. That's probably what I'd do, rather than learn the new stuff.

S1.say: I'd say there's always change and we'll see, without making a fuss in public. If asked, I'd say I'll learn what I need to when I need to.
S1.think: I'd be a bit worried, because the new die-cutters feed themselves and my job would turn into watching a screen. I think I'd be bad at that.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, saves a bit more each month and pushes the kitchen renovation back a year. Would take employer training if offered but wouldn't seek it out.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like waiting for news nobody can explain.
S1.quote: I can hear a jam coming two seconds before it happens. I can't hear a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Lena's worry is specific: losing the sensory feel she's built for her machine. Her fallback is to move to another plant still using old machines rather than adapt. She says one thing publicly and admits more worry privately, though the gap is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, someone should have stopped it. I'd say that the government and the companies both let it happen and now they've got to sort out the mess. I'd say it at work, maybe at Marco's mum's table, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be out of a job pretty quickly, and so would everyone at the plant. And it's not like I could just go to another box plant, because they'd all be doing the same thing. The three plants down the road were my backup plan, and they'd all be buying the same robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any extra spending straight away, no kitchen, no holiday. Put everything I could into savings. I'd lean on Marco, because I think electricians would last longer than me, and we'd see what happens before making any big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I don't panic easily, but I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have two years. Is there anything at all you'd try to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what. If it can do any job, then any course I start could be pointless by the time I finish. I'd rather hold on to my money than spend it on a course for a job that might not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Marco. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I've always paid my half of everything, it matters to me. I'd hate being the one who's not bringing anything in, even if he'd never say a word about it.

S2.say: I'd say it came too fast and someone should have stopped it. The government and the companies both let it happen, so they should sort out the mess.
S2.think: I think I'd lose my job quickly, and the other box plants nearby would all automate too. My backup plan of moving to another plant would be gone.
S2.do: Cuts all extra spending, including the kitchen and holidays, and puts everything she can into savings. Leans on Marco's electrician income and waits to see what happens before any big move.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, though she doesn't panic easily.
S2.quote: The three plants down the road were my backup plan, and they'd all be buying the same robots.
S2.fieldNote: Lena's fallback was other plants nearby, and fast AGI removes it, which is what alarms her. She would rather hold cash than retrain for something that might vanish. Being dependent on her partner bothers her more than the money itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not lose our heads. I'd probably say the government should help people find work that's still around. I'd keep it practical, no big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years makes it feel a bit less like a cliff. I'd have time to save more and maybe get into something that changes slowly. I'd be thirty-two, which isn't too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and save hard for a couple of years. Around year two or three I'd apply to the water treatment plant run by the council. I've heard they still use the same pumps from the eighties, and public places are slow to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the two-year one. More like a knot than a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the water plant, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco did some wiring there and said it was like going back in time. Some places are slow because they're careful, and right now careful sounds wonderful. I'd still be working machines, just old, steady ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the water plant safe in a world where AI can do almost any job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever. But councils take years to decide anything, so maybe it buys me five or ten more years. That's honestly the best plan I can think of.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so let's not lose our heads. The government should help people find work that's still around.
S3.think: Five years makes it feel less like a cliff. I'd have time to save more and move into work that changes slowly, and at thirty-two that isn't too late.
S3.do: Keeps her job and saves hard for two years, then applies around year two or three to the council-run water treatment plant, where she expects change to be slow.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a knot rather than a punch.
S3.quote: Some places are slow because they're careful, and right now careful sounds wonderful.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Lena finds a characteristic plan: move somewhere slower, not somewhere newer. She admits it's not safe forever but sees it buying time. She's honest that it's the best idea she has, not a perfect one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, and people shouldn't panic. I'd say the government should plan properly and give people time to adjust. Same as always, practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years would make it easy for me to put things off. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrived. I'd probably stay at the box plant for most of it, then make a move later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the plant for the first few years and keep saving. Around year five I'd look at the water plant or another slow public job. We'd still do the kitchen, maybe in year two, because ten years is too long to live with that cooker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Just more slowly. It'd always be sitting there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes it easy to put things off. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. I know myself. If you give me ten years to change, I'll spend nine of them hoping I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before you made a move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots actually working in a box plant like mine, not just a video from some showroom. When the manager starts walking people round with clipboards, that's when I'd go. I'd want to leave before they ask, not after.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare and people shouldn't panic. The government should plan properly and give people time to adjust.
S4.think: Ten years would make it easy for me to put things off. I'd probably stay at the box plant for most of the decade and only move near the end.
S4.do: Stays at the plant and keeps saving for the first few years, doing the kitchen in year two. Looks at the water plant or another slow public job around year five, once she sees robots actually arriving.
S4.feel: Anxious, but slowly, like a constant background worry.
S4.quote: If you give me ten years to change, I'll spend nine of them hoping I don't have to.
S4.fieldNote: Lena knows her own tendency to delay and says so plainly. Her trigger to move is concrete: managers walking round with clipboards. The ten-year picture doesn't calm her much, because the end point is the same.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It takes away my backup plan, which is all the other box plants, and gives me no time to find another one. I don't need much, I just need to know there's a next step. What would help is the government making sure there are steady jobs people can move into, even slow public ones, and some help with the cost while you move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the people who aren't good with technology would manage. Everyone assumes you can just learn it. Some of us are good at other things.

headlineQuote: I don't need much, I just need to know there's a next step.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old die-cutter operator at a cardboard box plant, sharing a flat with her electrician partner Marco and holding about eight months of savings. She learns with her hands and ears, has never used AI and quietly outlasted a tablet rollout at work. Her backup plan is the other box plants nearby, so she stays fairly calm until fast AGI threatens all of them at once, which alarms her. With five or ten years she plans to move to a slow-changing public job like the council water plant, while openly admitting she tends to put change off.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because it removes her backup plan of other local plants and leaves no time to find another.
whatWouldHelp: The government making sure there are steady jobs people can move into, even slow public ones, plus some help with costs while moving.
